THE QUEEN'S DEMOCRACY. o:PCli:sore the Queen's birthday han come and gone, and the citizens of this free country have not been slow to avail them- selves, so usual, of that right of free speech which is the admiration of envious foreign- er., and which enable. the Great, while living, to anticiyate the public verdict that never fails to be pronounced after they have ceased to bury themeelvee with "the works that are done under the enn." Some of the journalists who look forward eagerly to this I animal theme have really outdone them- selves on this occasion. And it must be ad- mitted that the topio of Royalty in Its personal and domestic relations and develop- ment. is far from being barren or uninvit- ing to the critical intelligence. One doesn't used to be 00th. staff of " The Irishman," or even of "Reynolds' Newspaper," to assume that the interest of the British tax- payer in the multiplication of a clam some of whose members are frankly alleged to lack adequate ram Pt, from the taxpaying point of view not being richly en- dowed with useful or ornamental attri- butee—is growingly sincere and lively. The " Graphic " preeented to its purchasers the other day a large engraving of the Royal Circle. If a reader of an arithmetical turn will count head., he will find, if we do not mistake, .forty save one."—exactly the num- ber of articles to which ingenuous Church- men yield the intellectual and moral homage of their "snout and consent." We have heard much of the hardships of " subecrip- tion," and we shall yet hear more. But, in the race of a too-prolitlo Royal family, the remedy of diseetablishment and dieendow- meet is even more difficult of application. Sett itur anibulando,—the French prefer revo- lutions, progress by jolts ; we English await the turn of events, and sail when wind and tide are fair. lii. coneoling to review the good points in the "situation," se the Spectator essayed to de last week. This candid critic notes the curious fact that " forty-three separate governments, ruling peoples in the five continents of the wort& acknowledge, by the same formal festivities, their subordination to the middle-aged lady who retreats from their homage to a High- land forest at the furthest extremity of her home dominion." The reign which is thus signalised has already lasted over forty years—that is to lay, it has outlasted a gen- eration of average-lived men. "The men who now rule no have passed from youth to maturity, from maturity to age, under the mine Sovereign, till she has become in their minds part of the natural order of things." . . The Queen does not govern, but she is. and all those who govern have to reckon with her." Nevertheless, "the long reign nod the steady, though probably un- conecioue influence of Queen Victoria have helped materially to smooth English pro- gress towards a Democratic organisation o the national life." Our contemporary goes on to arKUO that 'the idea of constitutional government has tinder her been modified in its whole charac- ter." This is partly owing to sex, partly to Whig education, but mainly to the excep- tional reasniableness of this Royal member of the Imperial executive. The Throne has come to be regarded, not as the foundation of the Constitution, but as a trusty pulley in the mechanism of State administration. Yet, the very freedom from dislike and cavil which has marked the Royal course ; the deference and popularity which have been enjoyed ; the dying out of all popular jealousy respecting prerogative, indicate an advance toward democracy, "make a Re- public much more nearly possible." • The gradual change in tho atmosphere of English social life has also given time for the aristocracy to die." The claim of birth has log its power. In the person of Lord Beaconsfield himself, democracy a very real sense—lifted into the highest place. Then the Queen's personal influence, so far as it has had room to operate, has been mostly in the Liberal direction— whether in her friendships or in her religi- ous leenings and association.. And freedom in such matters means the decay of monopoly and movement toward the demo- cratic ideal. The domestic graces and virtues of the Royal wife and widow have aided the growth of republican sentiment. There is MOTO of the middle-class appreciation of order and comfort, than of the heroic magnanimity of the Romeo patrician lady, about the life which divides itself chiefly between Balmoral and the Isle of Wight. Perham} the institution of monarchy in a diminishingly oppressive form, has a long lease to run. If so, it will be because the successors of Her Gracious Majesty have well learned the lesson of her long and prosperous life; because, yielding public service in return for conceded privilege, and narrowing more and more the circle of selfish pleasure, they worthily crown and ornament that edifice, whieh through the ages has been slowly and snrilly rising— " Broad-based upon the people's will, And compassed by the inviolate sea."
